content: Scombroid fish poisoning, also known as scombroid food poisoning, is a foodborne illness caused by the consumption of spoiled or decayed fish. This condition is most frequently associated with fish species such as tuna, mahi-mahi, bonito, sardines, anchovies, and other related species that have been improperly refrigerated or preserved after being caught. The poisoning typically results from inadequate handling of fish during storage or processing. The primary toxic agent implicated in scombroid poisoning is histamine, a chemical that accumulates in the fish due to bacterial breakdown of histidine, an amino acid found in muscle proteins. This process occurs through the increased production of the enzyme histidine decarboxylase. In addition to histamine, other by-products of this natural spoilage process may contribute to the toxic effects, although their exact role in scombroid poisoning has not been definitively established. Importantly, freezing, cooking, smoking, curing, or canning does not eliminate the potential toxins. Symptoms of scombroid poisoning can manifest within minutes to two hours after consuming the spoiled fish. These symptoms typically last for four to six hours and rarely persist beyond one to two days. Initial symptoms often mimic an allergic reaction and may include: Facial flushing and sweating A burning or peppery sensation in the mouth and throat Dizziness Nausea Headache Additional symptoms may develop and include: Facial rash Hives Edema (swelling) Short-term diarrhea Abdominal cramps Severe cases of scombroid poisoning can lead to: Blurred vision Respiratory distress Swelling of the tongue Treatment for scombroid poisoning typically involves the administration of antihistamines, which are prescribed by a physician to alleviate the symptoms.
